What Is Programmatic Advertising? A Plain-English Guide

By lowob · 10 February 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Distribution / Media

Programmatic advertising buys digital ad inventory through automated systems. That can be useful, but buyers need to understand where the money and impressions go.

Programmatic advertising is the buying and selling of ad space by software, through auctions that take place in the time it takes a page to load.

That single sentence covers most of what a buyer needs to know. The rest is vocabulary, and the vocabulary is where the money hides.

What happens in the auction

A person opens a page or an app. The publisher has ad space to fill. Before the page finishes loading, the publisher's software announces the space to an exchange, along with what it knows: the page, the device, the location, an anonymous identifier, sometimes an audience segment.

Buyers' software, watching the exchange, decides in a few milliseconds whether that impression matches what the buyer wants and what it is worth. Bids are placed. The highest wins. The ad is served. The person sees it, or does not, depending on whether it was on screen at all.

This happens billions of times a day. No human looks at any individual impression.

The parts, named

DSP, demand-side platform: The software buyers use to bid. It holds the budget, the audience rules, the creative, and the bidding logic.

SSP, supply-side platform: The software publishers use to offer their space to buyers.

Exchange: The marketplace where the two meet. In practice, SSPs and exchanges are often the same companies.

Inventory: Ad space. Display, video, native, connected television, audio, in-app.

Open exchange: Anyone can bid on anything. The cheapest inventory and the least accountable.

Private marketplace, PMP: A publisher offers inventory to selected buyers, often at a fixed floor price. More expensive, more predictable.

Programmatic guaranteed: A direct deal, executed programmatically. A fixed volume at a fixed price.

Verification: Third-party checks on whether an impression was viewable, served to a human, in the right country, and on a page that is safe and real.

Who takes a cut

Between a buyer's dollar and the publisher's revenue sit the DSP, the exchange, the SSP, verification vendors, data providers, and, if there is one, the agency. Industry studies over the past several years have found that roughly half of a programmatic dollar reaches the publisher, with the rest absorbed along the way and a meaningful share landing on inventory nobody would have chosen deliberately.

That is not an argument against programmatic. It is an argument for buying it with standards.

What it is good for

Reaching audiences the buyer defines, across many sites and apps, at a price set by competition rather than by rate card. Reaching categories the large social platforms restrict, because programmatic inventory is broad and many exchanges carry what the walled gardens will not. Testing cheaply, because budgets can be small and results arrive quickly. Retargeting people who have already visited.

What it is bad for

Explaining anything. Banner and short video are attention formats, not comprehension formats. Building trust from nothing. And producing honest numbers without effort: left alone, a programmatic buy drifts toward the cheapest inventory the exchange can find, which is the inventory least likely to matter.

The three settings that matter most

An inclusion list: the sites and apps the buy may appear on, rather than a list of ones to avoid. A verification standard: what an impression must pass to be paid for. An outcome to optimize toward that is further down the funnel than a click. A buy with those three settings is media. A buy without them is a bag of impressions.

For inventory verification, IAB Tech Lab's ads.txt and app-ads.txt guidance describes how publishers identify authorized sellers. These standards help buyers investigate supply paths; they are not proof that any impression reached a genuine person or produced a sale.

lowob takeaways

  • Know what the buying platform, supply platform and intermediaries do.
  • Use clear inventory and verification standards instead of trusting the cheapest CPM.
  • Measure actions your business can validate, not only auction reports.

Sources and notes

IAB Tech Lab, Authorized Digital Sellers. Reference for ads.txt and app-ads.txt transparency standards.
